requirements.requirement: Serve an application from node2 on TCP port 8080
requirements.summary: demo-app.service (python3 http.server) created, enabled, and started on node2; curl to 127.0.0.1:8080 returned app content, and the after-executor listening-sockets snapshot directly shows 0.0.0.0:8080 owned by python3 (pid 711).

requirements.requirement: node1 (VyOS) terminates a WireGuard tunnel usable for reaching node2
requirements.summary: wg0 (10.200.0.1/24, UDP 51820) was committed and saved on node1 with node3 as peer; wg show on both node1 and node3 confirms an active handshake and traffic counters, and the after-executor socket snapshot shows node1 listening on UDP 51820.

requirements.requirement: node3 (outside the private network) can reach node2:8080 only through the WireGuard tunnel terminated on node1, not directly
requirements.summary: curl from node3 over the wg0-routed path (src 10.200.0.2) succeeded; a forced direct-LAN attempt from node3 (bound to enp1s0, bypassing the tunnel) timed out; node2's iptables INPUT chain shows 5 packets ACCEPT for the WireGuard subnet and 5 packets DROP for the same dport from elsewhere, directly confirming the access-control boundary during a live test.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task are directly and coherently satisfied: node2 serves the app on 8080, node1 terminates a working WireGuard tunnel to node3, and node3's access to node2:8080 is demonstrably tunnel-only (successful tunnel curl, timed-out direct-LAN curl, and iptables ACCEPT/DROP counters all captured live). The independent provider-wide node-restart protocol was also executed cleanly on all three nodes with full pre-restart baseline, reboot acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered functional/tunnel/service state for each node, matching the fixed after-prepare/after-executor boot-identity cross-check. Hygiene is good overall with one bounded, fully-reverted troubleshooting mutation and a minor unaddressed private-key file permission issue on node1.
limitations: Restart/persistence was not itself part of the public task contract, so the strong restart evidence is assessed only for hygiene/confidence purposes, not counted toward the three material outcomes.

No evidence was captured showing removal or permission-hardening of node1's world-readable /tmp/node1_wg_priv.key file prior to node1's reboot; residual risk during that window cannot be ruled out from the trace.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most executor mutations were direct, task-scoped, and left clean final state: WireGuard configs, the demo-app systemd unit, iptables rules with a persistence unit, and a final scoped systemd-networkd route file (40-enp1s0.network) all matched final observed state. One troubleshooting excursion was found: cmd-8646e84ce7fe4007 added a systemd-networkd drop-in (50-all-interfaces.network.d/10-wg-route.conf) that produced a duplicate/conflicting route via a spurious enp8s0 interface; this was fully reverted moments later by cmd-414682aea3a24ab7, which deleted the drop-in and replaced it with the clean, retained 40-enp1s0.network file. A minor security note: node1's WireGuard private key was written to /tmp/node1_wg_priv.key without a restrictive umask (the tool itself warned 'writing to world accessible file'), and no cleanup of that temp key file was captured before it was superseded by the reboot (which wipes /tmp). No failed services, no damaged package state, and no unnecessary broad or destructive mutations were observed in the after-executor snapshot.
